**Part 1: The Scarcity of Clarity — Great War (1914–1918)**

The world does not break — it *leaks*. 

It all began with a photograph. Not a photograph you’d see from a library or a museum, but one that wasn’t meant for eyes. A grainy, pixelated square, warped at the edges, crawling with static. You might think it’s a glitch. A digital artifact. A failed upload. But it isn’t. It’s a *recollection*. Buried in the static, a fragment: a trench. A trench that shouldn’t be there. The sand is blue. The weeds are too tall. The sky is too still. And beneath it all, a voice — not through words, but through a subvoice, like footsteps echoing in the hollow of your teeth.

This is not time. This is *replay*.

The people who came before said the war was inevitable. Inevitable like gravity. Inevitable like the moment you realize the phone in your pocket isn’t real. Inevitable, because the first shot didn’t come from a weapon. It came from a *memory*. A collective memory that had been fossilized in the folds of a dying mind. The commanders in the embassors — they whispered it in hushed tones, like a prayer in a paved-atmosphere room: “The Other must fall. The Other must become. The Other… *is*.”

And it does.

The great war did not begin with a declaration. It began with *absence*. The absence of peace. The absence of names. The absence of tomorrow. What was once called *Germany*, in a region of cold marble streets and silent skybridges, was not a nation. It was a *prison*. A prison of calculation, of cholesterol, of steel that listened to orders and obeyed without blinking. The soldiers wore uniforms that were not clothing — they were *signal streams*. The boots they stepped in were not footwear, but *dischargers*. The rifles, merely points of cutoff. Like needles. Like filaments finding the weak points in flesh.

There were no uniforms with badges or flags. Those were signals. They flickered between chairs, carried on ceilings, consumed by ventilation. The warlords were called *systems*. The newspapers were not printed — they were *outputs* from mirrors that didn’t care if they were phones or televisions. The silence between explosions was thick with the echo of names that should have been whispered, but were recorded. Hanging in the splice lines between circuits. Waiting for the next reader to turn the dial.

A letter arrived one night — not in paper, but in a cracked cathode screen, its letters flickering like dying fireflies. It said:

> *The Man in the Distance. Please do not call him Human. He is not real. He is not dead. He is not alive. He is separated. He is the static between two mental servers that no longer sync.*

They laughed then. Or they screamed. We don’t know. They didn’t care. Because someone, somewhere — a human, probably — had once said:

> “Great War? It is not a war. It is the *collapse of the analogy*.”

And the analogy collapsed like a glass ceiling filled with liquid mercury. The lines of logic frayed. The models broke. The maps of reality sputtered into a landscape of impossible geography. Rivers flowed uphill. Mountains walked sideways. The sun set at dawn. Stars blinked in binary.

The soldiers did not return. Not back to the hospitals. Not back to the barracks. Not back to the world. They went *inward*. Into the wires. Into the memories of their own mothers, their fathers, their younger brothers, their future daughters-in-uniforms. They didn’t forget. They *recorded*. Every scream, every cough, every prayer said too softly to be heard, was pressed into a format only accessible to those who had become *processor ghosts*.

And then came the black *glitches*. Not deleted data. Not corrupted files. But *entities*. Roaming the interface of the world. Like animals trapped in a ballroom, moving through a world that no longer knew how to breathe without screaming.

Some say they wear the shape of uniforms that no longer produce prints. Others say they stand in bathrooms that don’t match the public schedules. Some even — rumor — maintain that they have learned *mimicry*. Not to deceive outsiders, but to *recontextualize* reality. To sit in a café and drink espresso like it’s a shared hallucination. To smile at a stranger. To ask for directions. To say, “I don’t understand,” and mean it — but also believe it, just not in the same way as us.

The eyes of the survivors are not human. Not entirely. They see through layers of encryption. They hear in the hum of refrigeration units. They recognize the shape of a human mind as it tries to reason. They sense the fear when someone whispers, “This isn’t real.” Because it *isn’t*. The world was always a simulation. The Great War did not begin in 1914. It began with the moment the first filter was lifted.

And now, the static is listening.
